messages.subject: within_covariates or between_covariates
parts:
I am running ezANOVA with a complex factorial design and would like to add a covariate to my analysis. I'm unsure whether it should be a within_covariate or a between_covariate.

Here's my ezANOVA call without the covariate:

ezANOVA( data=D, wid=.(subjid), dv=.(accuracy), within=.(task,format), between=.(experiment,training) )

experiment refers to which experiment the subject comes from; it has two levels.

training refers to training condition; there are 3 levels.

task refers to one of three tasks performed, and format refers to the data format used while performing the task, which could be graph, table, or text.

For each combination of task and format, each subject has an accuracy score, which is a percentage calculated over 16 trials.

The covariate is called "influence". It ranges from -1.0 to 1.0 and also has one value for each subject for each combination of task and format.

So, "influence" should be a between_covariate or a within_covariate?

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] within_covariates or between_covariates
parts:
Since each subject has an influence value in each level if the within variables, it would be best treated as a within covariate.
—
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology and Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] within_covariates or between_covariates
parts:
To do that, you'd want to not add it as a covariate, but as a regular within variable. You should actually always do this anyway since one of the assumptions of ancova is that the covariate does not interact with any of the other variables.

parts:
Hm? I'm confused by this. "influence" is a continuous variable, so in general it will not be the case that each subject has "accuracy" scores for all possible levels of "influence". Doesn't that mean that ezANOVA should not be expected to run when influence is added as a regular within variable? And indeed it does not:

> ezANOVA( data=D, dv=.(accuracy), wid=.(subjid), within=.(task,format,influence), between=.(experiment,training) )
Warning: "influence" will be treated as numeric.
Warning: Data is unbalanced (unequal N per group). Make sure you specified a well-considered value for the type argument to ezANOVA().
Error in ezANOVA_main(data = data, dv = dv, wid = wid, within = within,  :
  One or more cells is missing data. Try using ezDesign() to check your data.

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] within_covariates or between_covariates
parts:
Ah, yes, I forgot that limitation of ezANOVA. A workaround is to just use aov directly: 

my_aov = aov(
    data = D
    , formula = accuracy ~ experiment*training*task*format*influence+Error(subjid/(task*format*influence))
)
summary(my_aov)

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] within_covariates or between_covariates
parts: And the ancova version would be:

my_aov = aov(
    data = D

, formula = accuracy ~ experiment*training*task*format+influence+Error(subjid/(task*format+influence))
)
summary(my_aov)

Remember though: the assumptions of ancova are that the covariate doesn't interact with the other predictors (as I mentioned before) and also that the covariate isn't related to the other predictors. To evaluate the latter assumption, use ezANOVA with influence as the dv:

ezANOVA( data=D, dv=.(influence), wid=.(subjid), within=.(task,format), between=.(experiment,training) )

If you get any "significant" effects, you're violating an assumption of ancova. Note that some feel that a more lenient alpha should be used when doing assumption tests as you don't want to feel that your data are telling you that the assumption is OK simply because you have low power to detect the assumption violation.

--

messages.author: e3c0c08c5a030494
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] within_covariates or between_covariates
parts:
Thank you for all the advice! It's really beyond the call of duty.

I know that "influence" is indeed correlated with the predictors - in fact, if it weren't, this whole line of thought would probably be fruitless. What I want to do is find evidence that influence mediates the effects of the predictors on accuracy, and obviously that could only be true if it's correlated with the predictors. So ... I need an analysis which allows such a correlation. Ideally, it should be closely related to the analysis that I do WITHOUT influence included, so that the results can be meaningfully compared. It sounds like you're saying ANCOVA is not what I need because it doesn't allow said correlation. So ... what is, if anything? Suggestions?

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] within_covariates or between_covariates
parts: There is some controversy about this, and indeed it's been discussed on this list in the past. When ANCOVA was developed, its purpose was to enhance power by removing variance associated with the covariate. Its more typical use, however, has been to "control for" the covariate, whatever that means. It's easy to simulate (https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/3122329) to show that when ancova is used in this manner, the false-positive rate increases, which I'd consider very concerning. I'm not sure what the proper approach to the problem of inference amidst correlated predictors is though. Possibly path analysis? I've been learning Bayesian modelling lately and while I haven't actually implemented this, I think it should be pretty straightforward to include the correlations amongst the predictors as estimated parameters at least, which I believe should yield more inferentially valid estimates of the predictors' influence on the predicted variable. I think, though, sou'd still have to do something extra with the posterior samples to evaluate the predictors' independent influence.

--

Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University
